https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4n.text: Figure caption, Ukrainian vegetable seller targeted in 'human safari' drone attack By Laura Gozzi Published 4 August 2026, 17:11 BST Updated 2 hours ago Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared a video on social media of a drone hunting down a man in southern Ukraine, saying it showed an instance of a Russian "safari" attack against civilians. The video shows the drone pursuing a street vendor on a city street in the Kherson region. The man moves away from the drone hovering above, before it chases him as he runs around a white van. Eventually, the drone swoops down on him and explodes on impact. The man escaped with multiple shrapnel wounds, concussion and trauma, a doctor said. Sometimes called "human safari", the deployment of remotely-operated drones against civilians has often been used by Russians to terrify residents of front line areas in Ukraine. "The world must see this," Zelensky wrote on Telegram. "It must see every piece of evidence that Russia has gone mad, and every fact that Russian soldiers are enjoying killings and tormenting people." The video showed a "barbaric war crime", said Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. The safaris were a "deliberate and systemic Russian strategy," Sybiha said. "The sadist operating this drone knows full well that he is targeting a civilian." He added the attack was part of a deliberate Russian campaign to intimidate civilians and demanded international condemnation. The Kherson regional governor later posted a video showing the man - identified as Yuriy, a 52-year-old street vegetable vendor - speaking from a hospital bed following the drone attack. Yuriy said he and his wife had started to lay out crates of vegetables next to his van when he heard a distinctive buzzing sound overhead. When his wife ran away, the drone turned to him instead. He held up some heads of garlic towards the drone's camera to show the operator that he was not trying to film it. "It could see that I had tomatoes out, some cucumbers and eggplants laid out on the floor," Yuriy said. "It even ducked under the umbrella when I was running away round the other side." BBC Verify geolocated the video to a market space beside a roundabout in the Tavriiskyi district in northern Kherson. It is not clear who filmed the attack, or how - but the earliest public copy BBC Verify found was shared by a pro-Ukrainian Instagram account on Tuesday morning. "Safari" attacks have long been carried out by Russian troops in Kherson, which sits only a few miles from the front line. A 2025 UN report said it had found Russian armed forces "recurrently killed and injured civilians" in the area by using drones to target them. The videos filmed by the drones before they explode on to their targets are often posted online, allowing thousands to witness the last moments of the terrified victims. "Posting videos of civilians being killed and injured amounts to the war crime of outrages upon personal dignity," the UN said. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and denies targeting civilians. https://english.radio.cz/czech-public-he.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Czech public health institute website still offline after weekend cyberattack Facebook Twitter The website of the National Institute of Public Health (SZÚ), which was targeted by hackers on Saturday evening, will remain offline for at least another 48 hours, the Health Ministry-run institution said on Sunday. The institute said the website was taken offline to allow a forensic analysis. It added that no sensitive data had been compromised and its operations had not been affected because the website is hosted externally. The National Institute of Public Health is a scientific and expert body responsible for monitoring the spread of diseases, studying the impact of the environment on public health, and supporting disease prevention and control in the Czech Republic. https://www.cosmopolitan.com/entertainme.text: Calling all true crime fans! Netflix’s latest addition of the Monster anthology series is here, bringing to our screens a dramatization of the life of Lizzie Borden, who was accused of murdering her parents with an ax.Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story dropped on Netflix on September 17, and following in the tradition of the previous Monster series, it explores Lizzie's alleged crime and the lead-up that caused her to enact her revenge.For those not familiar with Lizzie's tale, Lizzie Borden was a woman in her early thirties in 1892 when she allegedly brutally killed both her father and stepmom with an ax in their Massachusetts home. While put on trial for their murders, she was not found guilty and went on to live her life until her death at age sixty-six.However, Andrew and Abby Borden's savage deaths have lived on in public imagination, as has Lizzie's status as a killer, despite being found innocent. The Monster series imagines what could have led Lizzie to kill her family. Early on in the series they show Lizzie hearing a story from her maid Bridget about a female serial killer from the sixteenth century—Elizabeth Báthory.But was this Countess actually a murderer? Here's the true story behind the tale.Who is Elizabeth Báthory in Netflix's Monster? During the first episode of Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, after new maid Bridget (Vicky Krieps) moves into the Borden household, she tells Lizzie (Ella Beattie) the story about a Countess called “Elizabetta Comtesse de Sang” aka the Blood Countess.In these scenes, Elizabetta (played by Krieps) is the richest woman in her kingdom in Transylvania and was obsessed with maintaining her beauty. She would bathe in gallons of cow's milk in order to smooth her complexion.However, she wasn't satisfied with milk and so she invited a group of the town's most beautiful virgins to dinner, feeding them meat in order to make their blood full of iron before killing the women in order to bathe in their blood. It's a story that then inspires Lizzie to bathe in a bath of cherry juice.Who was the real Elizabeth Báthory? Er, so did this Countess really bathe in the blood of virgins? Well, we do know for sure that the Countess existed and lived from 1560–1614.She was born in Transylvania (now part of Romania) to a wealthy family and was exposed to violence at a young age, with one source claiming she watched a public execution at age six. During her childhood she was also said to have suffered from "epileptic seizures, violent mood swings, as well as painful migraines," according to National Geographic.When she was fifteen, she got married to Count Ferenc Nádasdy, lived in western Hungary and the pair had four children.According to reports, Elizabeth’s husband encouraged cruelty to their servants and would set up various tortures for Elizabeth to watch, enjoy and take part in. This continued for years, with the pair indulging in torture, and their notoriety became so widespread that villagers were said to have hidden their daughters.After her husband died in 1604, Elizabeth continued her torture, but also extended her victims to those of the noble class and it was after this that investigations began on behalf of the king into the high number of deaths at her castles.She was later arrested and imprisoned for the murder of eighty women, however, some argued it was closer to 600 but she was never convicted. Instead, she spent her remaining days locked in a prison cell, where she eventually died in 1614.However, some scholars believe the reports of Elizabeth’s crimes are unsubstantiated and in fact were "political slander" by members of her family who were intent on getting their hands on her land and fortune, which they would be able to do if she were imprisoned.As for bathing in the blood of virgins, there is no historical evidence to suggest this happened for certain.Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is available to stream on Netflix now.

He also accused Vladimir Putin of showing no genuine interest in peace talks and urged European allies to increase support for Kyiv. Zelenskyy criticized Trump's Russia diesel deal for funding war. He accused Putin of stalling peace talks and faking negotiations. Zelenskyy urged EU leaders for €70 billion in extra support. Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday criticised US President Donald Trump’s deal allowing Russia to supply diesel to the US and global markets, warning that the arrangement would channel more money to Moscow to fund its war against Ukraine. He also accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of having no genuine interest in peace negotiations, describing Moscow’s approach as a “parody” of efforts to end the conflict. Speaking on the sidelines of a European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy welcomed a greater role for European allies in peace efforts and urged the bloc to provide Ukraine with additional financial and military support. “And now we can see how cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal,” Zelenskyy told reporters, according to Reuters. “This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets. But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war,” he added. Zelenskyy said Moscow was not interested in negotiations to end the war. “Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form,” he said. “He’s playing with words, claiming they respond... Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war.” The diesel agreement has strained relations between Kyiv and Washington. Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for pushing up global energy prices, with the US midterm elections approaching in November. Trump had announced that Ukraine and Russia agreed not to attack each other’s energy infrastructure. However, Zelenskyy subsequently declared the energy truce over, citing continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian refineries on Thursday. Trump called the Ukrainian strikes a “disgrace” in an interview with Newsmax, saying they were driving up global oil prices. The Kremlin, meanwhile, said Ukraine had undermined the possibility of an immediate resumption of peace talks by launching drone attacks on Moscow during the previous month’s election. This was Moscow’s account of why negotiations had stalled. Ukraine seeks more European financial support Zelenskyy urged European leaders to provide Ukraine with at least €70 billion in additional support next year for defence, weapons and resilience. “The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said in an address to EU leaders that he later posted on X. “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back,” he added. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told Reuters that the European Union would probably need to extend another loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget shortfall next year. “Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said. On arriving at the summit, Zelenskyy referred to his European counterparts as “real leaders”. Asked whether he felt Trump was making him a scapegoat for high energy prices and the course of the Iran war, he paused, smiled and replied, “This is my answer,” drawing laughter from the room. EU leaders were also divided over how to address rising energy prices linked to the Iran war and finalise the bloc’s budget. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said on Friday that member states remained “incredibly far apart” on the EU budget. Starshield disruption raises concerns Zelenskyy said disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system had improved but were not fully resolved, warning that the interruption put civilians at risk. Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service, supports Ukrainian battlefield communications and drone operations. A US official denied that Trump had ordered a deliberate slowdown of the system, while Trump said intelligence sharing with Ukraine was continuing. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe could not replace the system’s capabilities in the short term. “Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in the short term, Europe can’t replace this capability,” she said. The summit took place as Russian attacks continued across Ukraine. Drone strikes on Kharkiv killed three people, while attacks elsewhere left hundreds of thousands without electricity.
